facts.text: Amoreiras hosts the historic Mãe d'Água reservoir, a 19th‑century water tank that now forms part of Lisbon’s Museu da Água network.
The reservoir’s interior features a cascading water inlet that feeds a central cistern, creating one of Lisbon’s most distinctive hydraulic interiors.
The aqueduct that feeds the reservoir, the Águas Livres Aqueduct, was engineered by Hungarian architect Carlos Mardel in the mid‑1700s.
Amoreiras is home to the post‑modern Amoreiras Towers, designed by Tomás Taveira and unveiled in the mid‑1980s, a sharp contrast to the historic aqueduct.
The old Royal Silk Factory in Amoreiras now houses the Fundação Arpad Szenes – Vieira da Silva, a museum dedicated to two of Portugal’s most significant modernist painters.
Guided tours of Lisbon’s aqueducts often include access to the Mãe d’Água reservoir, explaining how the city’s water system shaped its growth.
